topics.name: Basic economic ideas and resource allocation

questions.q: A positive statement is one that…
questions.why: Normative statements contain opinions about what ought to be.

questions.q: The ceteris paribus assumption means…
questions.why: It isolates the effect of one variable.

questions.q: In a mixed economy, resources are allocated by…
o: both the market and the state
questions.why: Most economies combine private markets with public provision.

questions.q: An economy has unemployed workers. How is this shown on a production possibility curve?
o: A shift of the PPC to the left
A shift of the PPC to the right
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common error was shifting the PPC left rather than showing a point inside the curve.

questions.q: An economy on its production possibility curve moves from 60 cars and 40 tractors to 50 cars and 60 tractors. What is the opportunity cost of each extra tractor?
questions.why: 10 cars are given up to gain 20 tractors, so each extra tractor costs 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 cars.

long.q: Use a production possibility curve to explain the meaning of opportunity cost.
scheme: B1: opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up
B1: a PPC shows the combinations of two goods that can be made with all resources fully used
B1: moving along the curve, making more of one good means making less of the other: that amount is the opportunity cost

long.q: Distinguish between positive and normative statements, using an example of each about a national minimum wage.
scheme: B1: a positive statement is about facts: it can be tested against evidence
B1: example, e.g. 'raising the minimum wage by 10% will reduce employment of young workers by 2%'
B1: a normative statement is a value judgement about what ought to be: it cannot be tested
B1: example, e.g. 'the minimum wage should be raised because low-paid workers deserve more'

long.q: Explain how resources are allocated in a market economy, and one reason why this may lead to an unequal distribution of income.
scheme: B1: resources are allocated by the price mechanism, through the decisions of consumers and producers
B1: consumers' spending signals what they want; higher prices give firms an incentive to supply more of it
B1: resources move to where profits are highest, deciding what, how and for whom to produce
B1: income depends on the factors a person owns and their price, so those with scarce skills, land or capital earn far more than others

long.q: Explain why a public good such as street lighting would not be provided by a free market.
scheme: B1: it is non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting
B1: it is non-rival: one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others
B1: so consumers have an incentive to be free riders and will not pay
B1: firms cannot make a profit, so there is a missing market

long.q: Explain what is meant by the division of labour, giving two advantages and one disadvantage of it.
scheme: B1: division of labour: production is split into separate tasks, each done by a different worker
B1: an advantage, e.g. workers become skilled at their task, so output per worker rises
B1: a second advantage, e.g. less time lost moving between tasks / easier to use specialised machinery / shorter training
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. repetitive work lowers motivation / production stops if one stage fails / workers have few transferable skills

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand is negative. The good is…
questions.why: Demand for inferior goods falls as income rises.

questions.q: Cross elasticity of demand between two goods is positive. They are…
questions.why: A rise in one's price raises demand for the other.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is…
o: the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they pay
questions.why: It is the area below the demand curve and above the price.

questions.q: If demand is price inelastic, a price rise will…
questions.why: Quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.

questions.q: Incomes rise by 5% and the quantity demanded of a good rises by 10%. What is its income elasticity of demand and what type of good is it?
o: +2, a normal good that is income elastic
questions.why: YED = +10% ÷ +5% = +2; a positive value shows a normal good, and a value above 1 means demand is income elastic.

long.q: When the price of a good rises from $10 to $12, the quantity demanded falls from 500 to 450 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and explain what happens to total revenue.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity = −10%; % change in price = +20%
B1: demand is price inelastic
B1: total revenue rises, from $5000 to $5400

long.q: The price of coffee rises by 8% and, as a result, the quantity demanded of tea rises by 6%. Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for tea with respect to the price of coffee and explain what it shows.
scheme: M1: XED = % change in quantity demanded of tea ÷ % change in price of coffee = 6 ÷ 8
B1: positive, so the goods are substitutes; less than 1, so they are not very close substitutes

long.q: A market has a straight-line demand curve on which quantity demanded is zero at a price of $20 and 100 units at a price of $0. The supply curve is a straight line starting at a price of $2 at zero output. The equilibrium price is $8. Calculate the consumer surplus and the producer surplus at equilibrium.
scheme: M1: demand: P = 20 − 0.2Q, so at P = $8, Q = 60 units
M1: consumer surplus = ½ × 60 × (20 − 8)
M1: producer surplus = ½ × 60 × (8 − 2)

long.q: Demand for electric cars increases. Explain how the signalling, incentive and rationing functions of the price mechanism reallocate resources in this market.
scheme: B1: signalling: the rise in demand causes excess demand, so the price rises, signalling that consumers want more
B1: incentive: higher prices raise expected profit, so firms move resources into making more electric cars (extension of supply)
B1: rationing: the higher price reduces quantity demanded, so the cars go to those most willing and able to pay
B1: a new equilibrium is reached at a higher price and quantity, with resources moved from other uses

long.q: Explain why the price elasticity of supply of many farm products is lower in the short run than in the long run.
scheme: B1: in the short run supply is fixed by what was planted: crops take months to grow
B1: farmers cannot quickly add land or capital, and many products cannot be stored, so supply is price inelastic
B1: in the long run farmers can change what they plant, bring in more land and machinery, and new farmers can enter
B1: so quantity supplied responds more to price: PES is higher

questions.q: An indirect tax on a good with inelastic demand falls mainly on…
questions.why: Producers can pass most of the tax on as higher prices.

questions.q: A negative externality of production leads a free market to…
questions.why: Firms ignore external costs, so marginal social cost exceeds private cost.

questions.q: A public good is…
questions.why: These features create the free-rider problem.

questions.q: A specific tax of $4 per unit is imposed and the market price rises from $10 to $13. How is the burden of the tax shared?
o: Consumers $3 per unit, producers $1 per unit
Consumers $1 per unit, producers $3 per unit
Consumers $2 per unit, producers $2 per unit
questions.why: Consumers pay $3 more per unit; producers receive $13 − $4 = $9, which is $1 less than before.

questions.q: A government sets a minimum price for wheat above the equilibrium price. What is the most likely result?
o: A shortage and a black market
A surplus that the government may have to buy up
questions.why: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so there is excess supply that must be stored, bought or destroyed.

long.q: Explain why a maximum price set below the equilibrium price may lead to a shortage and a black market.
scheme: B1: at the lower price quantity demanded rises
B1: and quantity supplied falls
B1: so there is excess demand (a shortage)
B1: some buyers will pay more than the legal price, so goods are sold illegally above it

long.q: Before a specific tax, a good sold 1000 units at $20. After a tax of $5 a unit, the price rises to $23 and 900 units are sold. Calculate the government's tax revenue and the amount of the tax paid by consumers and by producers.
scheme: B1: tax revenue = 5 × 900 = $4500
M1: consumers pay 23 − 20 = $3 of each $5 tax; producers pay $2
A1: consumers' share = 3 × 900 = $2700
A1: producers' share = 2 × 900 = $1800

long.q: A government gives a subsidy to producers of solar panels. Explain the effect on the market and one possible problem with the policy.
scheme: B1: the subsidy lowers producers' costs, so supply shifts to the right (down by the amount of the subsidy)
B1: the price falls and the quantity bought and sold rises
B1: if solar panels give external benefits (less pollution), consumption moves closer to the socially optimum level
B1: a problem, e.g. the opportunity cost of the government spending / hard to set the right size / firms may become inefficient or keep part of the subsidy

long.q: Explain why information failure may lead to over-consumption of a demerit good, and one policy a government could use to correct it.
scheme: B1: consumers underestimate the harm the good does to them, e.g. the health effects of smoking
B1: so their private demand is higher than it would be with full information
B1: consumption is greater than the socially optimum level, so resources are misallocated
B1: a policy, e.g. advertising campaigns / health warnings / an indirect tax / a ban on advertising, explained

long.q: Assess whether direct provision by the government is the best way to make sure that enough healthcare is consumed.
scheme: B1: healthcare is a merit good: without intervention it is under-consumed
B1: direct provision free at the point of use removes the price barrier, so consumption rises, including by the poor
B1: a drawback, e.g. high cost to taxpayers / opportunity cost / excess demand and waiting lists
B1: a further drawback, e.g. state provision may lack the incentive to be efficient (government failure)
B1: an alternative, e.g. subsidies, vouchers, regulation or information campaigns
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. depends on cost, efficiency and the government's equity aims

questions.q: Aggregate demand is…
questions.why: Consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

questions.q: Cost-push inflation is caused by…
o: rising costs of production, such as wages or oil
questions.why: Higher costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

questions.q: Which is counted as unemployed?
o: Someone able and willing to work and actively seeking work
questions.why: The ILO definition requires being without work, available and looking.

questions.q: On an AD/AS diagram, what should the axes be labelled?
o: Price level and real output (real GDP)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many labelled the axes 'price' and 'quantity' and the curves 'D' and 'S' instead of AD and AS.

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is best explained as:
o: A rise in costs of production
A fall in the money supply
An increase in AD not matched by spare capacity in AS
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not refer to AD, or did not say the AD rise is not matched by spare capacity.

long.q: Distinguish between demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
scheme: B1: demand-pull: aggregate demand rises faster than aggregate supply / the economy's capacity
B1: an example cause: rising consumer spending, lower interest rates, more government spending
B1: cost-push: rising costs of production push up the price level (AS shifts left)
B1: an example cause: higher wages, oil or import prices, a weaker exchange rate

long.q: A country's nominal GDP rose from $500 billion to $540 billion in a year, while the price index (GDP deflator) rose from 100 to 105. Calculate real GDP in the second year at the first year's prices and the rate of real economic growth.
scheme: A1: = $514.3 billion

long.q: Explain the difference between gross domestic product (GDP) and gross national income (GNI).
scheme: B1: GDP is the value of output produced within a country in a year, whoever owns the factors
B1: GNI is GDP plus net primary income from abroad (income earned abroad by residents minus income paid to foreigners)
B1: example, e.g. profits of foreign-owned firms sent home reduce GNI below GDP

long.q: Explain two factors that could shift a country's aggregate supply curve to the right.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. a fall in costs of production such as wages or imported raw materials
B1: explained: firms can supply more at every price level (short-run AS shifts right)
B1: a second factor, e.g. an increase in the quantity or quality of resources (investment, technology, education, immigration)
B1: explained: productive capacity rises, so long-run AS shifts right

long.q: Explain two costs of high inflation for an economy.
scheme: B1: one cost, e.g. the country's exports become less price competitive
B1: explained: export sales fall and imports rise, worsening the current account
B1: a second cost, e.g. uncertainty reduces investment / menu and shoe-leather costs / redistribution from savers and those on fixed incomes
B1: explained with its effect on the economy, e.g. lower investment reduces future growth

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy involves…
o: raising government spending or cutting taxes
questions.why: It boosts aggregate demand.

questions.q: Supply-side policies aim to…
o: increase the productive capacity of the economy
questions.why: Examples: education, training, deregulation, infrastructure.

questions.q: Which is an example of expansionary fiscal policy?
questions.why: Fiscal policy uses tax and spending; monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply.

questions.q: Which policy aims to reduce a current account deficit through expenditure-switching rather than expenditure-reducing?
questions.why: Tariffs make imports dearer, switching spending towards domestic goods; the other policies reduce total spending, including on imports.

questions.q: Which is an example of a conflict between macroeconomic objectives?
o: Cutting income tax may raise both employment and growth
Supply-side policies may lower inflation and unemployment together
Cutting interest rates to reduce unemployment may raise inflation
Higher productivity may improve both growth and the current account
questions.why: Lower interest rates raise aggregate demand, which reduces unemployment but can push up the price level, so one objective is traded off against another.

long.q: Explain how a rise in the central bank's rate of interest might reduce inflation.
scheme: B1: borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more rewarding
B1: so consumption and investment fall
B1: aggregate demand falls (also via a stronger exchange rate cutting net exports)
B1: so demand-pull pressure on the price level eases

long.q: In a recession, government spending is $250 billion and tax revenue $230 billion, and GDP is $1000 billion. Calculate the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP and explain two reasons why a deficit tends to grow during a recession.
scheme: A1: = 2% of GDP
B1: tax revenue falls as incomes, spending and profits fall
B1: government spending on unemployment and other benefits rises

long.q: Explain how privatisation could be used as a supply-side policy to increase an economy's productive capacity.
scheme: B1: privatisation transfers ownership of state-owned firms to the private sector
B1: private owners have a profit motive, so an incentive to cut costs and use resources efficiently
B1: the firms can raise finance from shareholders for investment and new technology
B1: higher productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply (the PPC) outwards

long.q: Explain why an expansionary fiscal policy to reduce unemployment may conflict with the aim of a sustainable current account.
scheme: B1: higher government spending or lower taxes raise aggregate demand
B1: output rises, so firms employ more workers and unemployment falls
B1: but higher incomes increase spending on imports
B1: and rising demand may cause inflation, making exports less competitive, so the current account worsens

long.q: Distinguish between expenditure-reducing and expenditure-switching policies to correct a current account deficit, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: expenditure-reducing policies cut total spending in the economy, so spending on imports falls
B1: example, e.g. higher income tax / lower government spending / higher interest rates
B1: expenditure-switching policies make imports dearer relative to home-produced goods, so spending switches to domestic goods
B1: example, e.g. tariffs / quotas / a devaluation of the currency

questions.q: Comparative advantage means a country should specialise where it has…
questions.why: Trade can benefit both countries even if one is better at everything.

questions.q: The Marshall–Lerner condition states a depreciation improves the current account if…
questions.why: Sum of export and import price elasticities (absolute values) must exceed 1.

questions.q: On a diagram of a currency market, the vertical axis is:
o: The exchange rate (price of the currency)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many labelled the vertical axis 'price' rather than the price of the currency or exchange rate.

questions.q: Where are remittances from workers abroad recorded in the balance of payments?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 39% chose the wrong option; remittances are current transfers, recorded in secondary income.

questions.q: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 110 while its import price index rises from 100 to 125. What is its terms of trade index?
questions.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 110 ÷ 125 × 100 = 88, a deterioration.

long.q: A worker in Country A can make 10 units of wheat or 5 units of cloth. A worker in Country B can make 6 units of wheat or 6 units of cloth. Explain which country has a comparative advantage in each good.
scheme: M1: opportunity cost of 1 cloth: A gives up 2 wheat, B gives up 1 wheat
M1: opportunity cost of 1 wheat: A gives up 0.5 cloth, B gives up 1 cloth
B1: A has the comparative advantage in wheat
B1: B has the comparative advantage in cloth, so each should specialise and trade

long.q: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 108, while its import price index falls from 100 to 96. Calculate its terms of trade index and explain why this change may not benefit the country.
scheme: M1: terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 108 ÷ 96 × 100
B1: an improvement: each unit of exports buys more imports
B1: but if demand for exports is price elastic, export volumes and revenue fall, worsening the current account and jobs

long.q: Explain the difference between the current account and the financial account of the balance of payments.
scheme: B1: the current account records trade in goods and services and flows of income
B1: e.g. exports and imports, primary income (profits, interest, wages) and secondary income (remittances, aid)
B1: the financial account records flows of investment and changes in ownership of financial assets
B1: e.g. foreign direct investment, portfolio investment and changes in reserves

long.q: Explain how a rise in a country's rate of interest relative to other countries might affect its floating exchange rate.
scheme: B1: saving in the country becomes more attractive, so short-term capital (hot money) flows in
B1: foreigners need the currency, so demand for it rises (and supply falls as residents save at home)
B1: the exchange rate appreciates

long.q: Assess the infant industry argument for protection.
scheme: B1: a new industry has high average costs because it cannot yet benefit from economies of scale
B1: protection, e.g. tariffs, gives it time to grow and lower its costs until it can compete
B1: it may later gain a comparative advantage, bringing jobs, growth and exports
B1: a weakness: protected firms have little incentive to become efficient, so protection may never be removed
B1: a further weakness, e.g. consumers pay higher prices / other countries may retaliate / hard to pick winners
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. justified only if temporary and clearly targeted

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy (A Level)

questions.q: A firm maximises profit where…
questions.why: Producing one more unit would add more to cost than to revenue beyond that point.

questions.q: In perfect competition in the long run, firms earn…
questions.why: Free entry and exit remove supernormal profit.

questions.q: A natural monopoly arises because of…
o: economies of scale so large that one firm has the lowest cost
questions.why: Examples include water and electricity grids.

questions.q: At its profit-maximising output, a perfectly competitive firm faces a price of $10, average cost of $12 and average variable cost of $9. What should it do in the short run?
o: Shut down immediately, because it makes a loss
Keep producing, because price covers average variable cost
Increase output until price equals average cost
questions.why: Price above AVC means each unit adds something towards fixed costs, so the loss is smaller than shutting down; a price-taker cannot raise its price.

questions.q: In the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, prices tend to be stable because…
o: rivals follow a price rise but ignore a price cut
firms always collude openly to fix prices
rivals match a price cut but ignore a price rise
questions.why: A price rise loses customers to rivals who keep prices down, while a cut is matched and gains little, so firms have no incentive to change price.

long.q: Explain why a profit-maximising monopolist produces where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, and why this may be allocatively inefficient.
scheme: B1: below MC = MR, extra units add more to revenue than cost
B1: beyond it, extra units add more to cost than revenue
B1: allocative efficiency needs P = MC
B1: the monopolist's price is above MC, so output is restricted

long.q: A firm has total fixed costs of $400. Its total costs are $520 for 1 unit, $600 for 2 units, $660 for 3 units and $760 for 4 units. Calculate the marginal cost of the third and of the fourth unit and the average variable cost of 4 units, and explain why marginal cost eventually rises in the short run.
scheme: B1: marginal cost of the third unit = 660 − 600 = $60
B1: marginal cost of the fourth unit = 760 − 660 = $100
B1: average variable cost at 4 units = (760 − 400) ÷ 4 = $90
B1: the law of diminishing returns: as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the marginal product falls, so marginal cost rises

long.q: A consumer spends all her income on two goods: X costs $2 and Y costs $4. At her current purchases the marginal utility of X is 10 and that of Y is 16. Explain whether she is maximising her total utility and, if not, how she should change her spending.
scheme: M1: marginal utility per $: X = 10 ÷ 2 = 5; Y = 16 ÷ 4 = 4
A1: these are not equal, so she is not maximising utility
B1: she should buy more X and less Y, as the last $ spent on X gives more utility
B1: as she does so MU of X falls and MU of Y rises until MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py (the equi-marginal principle)

long.q: Explain the conditions necessary for a firm to practise price discrimination, and one way consumers may benefit from it.
scheme: B1: the firm must have some monopoly power: it is a price maker
B1: it must be able to separate the market into groups with different price elasticities of demand
B1: it must prevent resale between the groups (no seepage)
B1: a benefit, e.g. some consumers pay lower prices (students, off-peak) / extra profit makes a service viable or funds research

long.q: A proposed railway has private costs of $300 million and private benefits of $280 million. It would also cause external costs of $40 million and external benefits of $110 million. Calculate the net social benefit and explain why the government might build it even though a private firm would not.
scheme: M1: social cost = 300 + 40 = $340 million; social benefit = 280 + 110 = $390 million
A1: net social benefit = +$50 million
B1: a private firm considers only private costs and benefits, a net loss of $20 million, so would not build it
B1: the government considers external effects (e.g. less road congestion), so building it improves allocative efficiency (cost–benefit analysis)

questions.q: The Gini coefficient measures…
questions.why: 0 means perfect equality; 1 means maximum inequality.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when…
o: intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources
questions.why: Causes include poor information and unintended consequences.

questions.q: Why might a government provide education even though it is excludable?
o: It is a merit good with positive externalities that would be under-consumed
questions.why: Examiners (2023): link merit goods, positive externalities and allocative efficiency.

questions.q: A national minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market. What is the most likely effect?
o: Unemployment, as more labour is supplied than demanded
questions.why: At the higher wage, firms demand less labour while more people want to work, creating excess supply of labour.

questions.q: A worker on a means-tested benefit gets a pay rise, but loses benefit and pays more tax, so she is barely better off. What is this an example of?
questions.why: The withdrawal of benefits plus extra tax creates a very high effective marginal tax rate, reducing the incentive to earn more.

long.q: A firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market at $5 a unit and hires labour in a perfectly competitive labour market at a wage of $70 a day. Total output per day with 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 workers is 20, 38, 54, 66 and 75 units. Calculate the marginal revenue product of each worker and the number of workers the firm will employ.
scheme: M1: marginal product: 20, 18, 16, 12, 9
M1: MRP = MP × price
A1: employ 3 workers: the third adds $80 ≥ $70, the fourth only $60

long.q: Explain how a system of tradable pollution permits can reduce pollution at the lowest cost.
scheme: B1: the government sets a limit on total pollution and issues that number of permits
B1: firms that pollute less than their permits allow can sell spare permits to other firms
B1: firms that can cut pollution cheaply do so and sell permits; those for which it is costly buy them
B1: so the target is met where cutting pollution costs least, and permits can be reduced over time

long.q: Explain two causes of government failure when a government intervenes in markets.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. imperfect information: the government cannot measure external costs or benefits accurately
B1: explained: a tax or subsidy set at the wrong level leaves output away from the social optimum
B1: a second cause, e.g. unintended consequences (black markets, tax evasion) / administrative costs / political self-interest / regulatory capture
B1: explained: intervention makes resource allocation worse than before

long.q: Explain what a Lorenz curve shows, and how a fall in a country's Gini coefficient from 0.45 to 0.38 would appear on it.
scheme: B1: a Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentage of income against the cumulative percentage of the population
B1: the 45° line shows complete equality; the further the curve from it, the more unequal the distribution
B1: the Gini coefficient is the area between the line of equality and the curve divided by the whole area under the line
B1: a fall to 0.38 means less inequality, so the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality

long.q: Explain how a minimum wage set above the current wage in a monopsony labour market could raise both the wage and the level of employment.
scheme: B1: a monopsonist must raise the wage for all workers to hire one more, so the marginal cost of labour is above the average cost (supply) curve
B1: it employs where MCL = MRP and pays the lower wage on the supply curve, so wage and employment are below competitive levels
B1: a minimum wage makes the marginal cost of labour horizontal at that wage, up to the supply curve
B1: so the firm hires more workers, up to where the minimum wage = MRP, if it is set no higher than the competitive wage

questions.q: The multiplier is larger when the marginal propensity to consume is…
questions.why: In a closed economy without government, k = 1/(1 − MPC).

questions.q: The natural rate of unemployment is associated with…
questions.why: It exists when the labour market is in equilibrium.

questions.q: Which best describes long-run economic growth?
o: A rise in AD in the short run
A rise in the price level
An increase in the productive capacity of the economy (LRAS shifts right)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers stressed short-run growth from AD rather than potential growth from rising LRAS.

questions.q: The marginal propensities to save, to tax and to import are 0.1, 0.2 and 0.2. Investment rises by $5 billion. By how much does national income change?
questions.why: MPW = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.5, so the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 and income rises by 2 × 5 = $10 billion.

questions.q: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), if V and T are constant and the money supply rises by 8%, what happens to the price level?
questions.why: With V and T fixed, P changes in proportion to M, so an 8% rise in the money supply raises prices by 8%.

long.q: Explain how the multiplier works when government spending rises by $10 billion and the marginal propensity to withdraw is 0.25.
scheme: B1: multiplier = 1/MPW = 4
B1: national income rises by $40 billion
B1: each round of spending becomes someone's income, part of which is spent again
B1: withdrawals (saving, tax, imports) stop it rising for ever

long.q: A firm needs $4 of capital for each $1 of output a year. Its capital is fully used and there is no depreciation. Output rises from $100 million to $110 million, and the next year to $115 million. Calculate net investment in each year and explain what this shows about the accelerator.
scheme: M1: net investment = capital–output ratio × change in output
A1: first year: 4 × 10 = $40 million
A1: second year: 4 × 5 = $20 million
B1: investment depends on the change in output: when growth slows, investment falls even though output is still rising, which makes the economy more unstable

long.q: Explain the three motives for holding money in Keynes' liquidity preference theory, and how the demand for money is related to the rate of interest.
scheme: B1: transactions motive: money for everyday spending, which depends on income
B1: precautionary motive: money for unexpected spending, which also depends on income
B1: speculative motive: holding money rather than bonds, expecting bond prices to fall
B1: the speculative demand is inversely related to the interest rate: at higher rates the opportunity cost of holding money is greater, so less is held

long.q: Explain what is meant by a deflationary (negative output) gap and how a government could close it.
scheme: B1: actual output (national income) is below potential (full-employment) output
B1: so resources are unemployed; aggregate demand is too low
B1: it could be closed by raising AD, e.g. expansionary fiscal or monetary policy
B1: the increase in injections has a multiplier effect, so it need only be a fraction of the gap

long.q: Explain two reasons why rapid economic growth may not be sustainable.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. growth uses up non-renewable resources
B1: explained: future generations have fewer resources, so future output and living standards may fall
B1: a second reason, e.g. pollution and climate change / growth above the trend rate causes inflation and boom-bust
B1: explained with its cost to the economy

questions.q: Quantitative easing means the central bank…
o: buys financial assets to increase the money supply
questions.why: It aims to lower long-term interest rates and boost spending.

questions.q: What does the Phillips curve show in the short run?
o: A direct link between GDP and exports
An inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
A rise in both unemployment and inflation always
questions.why: In the long run it may be vertical at the natural rate.

questions.q: Which policy is supply-side?
o: Spending on training to raise labour productivity
questions.why: Supply-side policies aim to shift LRAS to the right.

questions.q: Which is an example of an automatic stabiliser?
o: A government announcing a new road-building programme
The central bank cutting its interest rate
A one-off cut in the rate of income tax
Tax revenue rising and benefit spending falling as incomes rise in a boom
questions.why: Automatic stabilisers change without any new decision, dampening the economic cycle; the other options are discretionary policy.

questions.q: According to the long-run (expectations-augmented) Phillips curve, what is the long-run effect of expansionary demand policy?
o: A permanent fall in unemployment with no extra inflation
Higher inflation with unemployment returning to its natural rate
questions.why: Once workers' inflation expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate, leaving only higher inflation; the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.

long.q: Assess whether supply-side policies are better than demand-side policies at reducing unemployment.
scheme: B1: supply-side: training, labour-market flexibility reduce structural unemployment
B1: but they take time and may be costly
B1: demand-side: fiscal or monetary expansion reduces cyclical unemployment quickly
B1: but risk inflation and do not fix structural problems
B1: a judgement depending on the cause of unemployment

long.q: Explain how quantitative easing is intended to increase aggregate demand.
scheme: B1: the central bank creates money electronically to buy bonds from banks and other financial institutions
B1: bond prices rise, so long-term interest rates (yields) fall
B1: banks have more reserves to lend and borrowing is cheaper
B1: so consumption and investment rise; higher asset prices also increase wealth and spending

long.q: Distinguish between automatic stabilisers and discretionary fiscal policy, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: automatic stabilisers change government spending and tax revenue without any new decision as national income changes
B1: example, e.g. in a recession benefit payments rise and income tax revenue falls, supporting demand
B1: discretionary policy is a deliberate decision to change spending or tax rates
B1: example, e.g. the government cuts VAT or spends more on infrastructure to boost demand

long.q: Assess whether cutting interest rates is effective in ending a deep recession.
scheme: B1: lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so consumption and investment should rise
B1: a weaker exchange rate raises net exports, adding to aggregate demand
B1: a limitation: in a deep recession low confidence means firms and households may not borrow (liquidity trap)
B1: a further limitation, e.g. rates may already be near zero / banks may not pass on the cut / time lags
B1: an alternative, e.g. expansionary fiscal policy or quantitative easing
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: Using Phillips curve analysis, assess whether a government can achieve both low inflation and low unemployment at the same time.
scheme: B1: the short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off: lower unemployment comes with higher inflation
B1: explained: higher demand reduces unemployment but bids up wages and prices
B1: in the long run the curve is vertical at the natural rate, as expectations of inflation adjust
B1: so demand-side policy cannot keep unemployment below the natural rate without rising inflation
B1: but supply-side policies can reduce the natural rate, shifting the curves left, so both can be lower
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. possible in the long run through supply-side policy, not through demand management alone

questions.q: Which measure of development adjusts income for differences in prices between countries?
questions.why: PPP compares how much a unit of income buys in each country.

questions.q: What does the Marshall–Lerner condition state?
o: Depreciation improves the current account if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1
questions.why: The J-curve shows it may worsen first.

questions.q: Which indicator measures development beyond income?
questions.why: HDI combines income, education and life expectancy.

questions.q: A country fixes its exchange rate against the US dollar. Market pressure starts to push its currency down. To keep the peg, the central bank is most likely to…
o: sell its own currency in exchange for foreign currency
buy its own currency using its foreign currency reserves
questions.why: Buying its own currency raises demand for it and supports the fixed rate; selling it or cutting interest rates would push it down further.

questions.q: Which indicator measures how many people in a country are deprived in health, education and living standards at the same time?
questions.why: The MPI counts overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards; the Gini coefficient measures income inequality only.

long.q: Explain the possible effects of a depreciation of a country's currency on its current account.
scheme: B1: exports become cheaper abroad, imports dearer at home
B1: export volumes rise, import volumes fall
B1: the current account improves if PED for exports and imports is elastic (Marshall–Lerner)
B1: J-curve: it may worsen first

long.q: A developing country's GDP per head is 60 million in its own currency. The market exchange rate is 15 000 units of its currency to $1 and the purchasing power parity rate is 5000 units to $1. Calculate GDP per head in US dollars using each rate and explain why they differ.
scheme: M1: GDP per head ÷ exchange rate
A1: at the market rate = 60 000 000 ÷ 15 000 = $4000
B1: prices, especially of non-traded goods and services, are lower in the developing country, so its income buys more there than the market rate suggests

long.q: Explain the meaning of trade creation and trade diversion when a country joins a customs union.
scheme: B1: trade creation: removing tariffs within the union lets a lower-cost member replace higher-cost domestic production
B1: so resources are used more efficiently and consumers pay lower prices
B1: trade diversion: the common external tariff means imports switch from a lower-cost country outside the union to a higher-cost member
B1: so world resources are used less efficiently

long.q: Assess the impact of multinational companies on the development of a developing economy.
scheme: B1: a benefit, e.g. foreign direct investment creates jobs and raises incomes
B1: a second benefit, e.g. transfer of technology and skills / tax revenue / exports improve the current account
B1: a cost, e.g. profits are sent back to the home country, so GNI rises less than GDP
B1: a second cost, e.g. local firms forced out / exploitation of labour or natural resources / pollution / tax avoidance
B1: depends on, e.g. the type of investment, local regulation, how far local suppliers are used
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage for a country of fixing its exchange rate.
scheme: B1: an advantage, e.g. certainty for exporters and importers, which encourages trade and investment
B1: a second advantage, e.g. discipline against inflation, as the government cannot rely on depreciation to restore competitiveness
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. large foreign currency reserves are needed to defend the rate
B1: explained, e.g. interest rates may have to be set to defend the rate rather than for domestic objectives
